newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-P&O, Stena join forces in Channel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-P&O, Stena join forces in Channel.

text.p: Rival ferry operators P&O of Britain and Sweden's Stena Line on Thursday unveiled battle plans to join forces on three routes in the English Channel in an offensive against the powerful Channel Tunnel.
"The tunnel is the enemy," Lord Sterling, chairman of Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O), told a news conference.
"It is a sort of David and Goliath if you like, but history has shown the world that David can win."
The companies confirmed months of market speculation by announcing proposals to combine services and cut costs by nearly 27 percent or 75 million pounds ($117.4 million).
That involves slashing at least 1,000 of 5,500 jobs and withdrawing two out of 15 ships.

The news came hours after Eurotunnel Plc/SA announced it had reached an outline deal with its banks over restructuring its massive debt burden. Details of the Eurotunnel restructuring are expected to be announced on Monday.
The merged ferry unit P&O Stena Line will be controlled equally, but P&O will hold 60 percent and Stena 40 percent of shares in the company.
With assets of 410 million pounds it has been designed to take on the battle fore supremacy across the world's busiest sea crossing.

Since late 1994 when Anglo-French Eurotunnel opened the tunnel, ferry operators have faced increasingly fierce competition on routes between Dover in Britain, Zeebrugge in Belgium and the French ports of Calais and Dieppe.

After slashing car tariffs by 50 percent in June, Eurotunnel in August secured 41 percent of car traffic on the Dover-Calais run against P&O and Stena's combined 41 percent, and 44 percent of freight against P&O Stena's 40 percent.
Other ferry operators on the Dover-Calais route are state-owned Sea France, Hoverspeed, owned by Sea Containers, and the newly merged Finnish-Australian line Holyman Sally.
The short-sea Channel routes are vital earners for the ferry companies that began talks in July after the British government lifted restrictions on cooperation between rival firms.
Stena managing director Bo Lerenius said the three routes in question accounted for 25 percent of his company's turnover and 50 percent of P&O European Ferries's revenue.
"We see a joint venture on the short-sea between P&O and Stena as possibly the only way to create a really strong and consistent competitor against the Eurotunnel," Lerenius said.
Analysts said the deal was seen as another positive move by Sterling who has tackled P&O's underperforming businesses with vigour.
P&O's share price reacted accordingly, jumping from 626 pence to a new year high of 657 before closing at 645. Stena shares rose more than two percent in Thursday trade.
"It is being viewed as a very positive deal and the pace at which Sterling is moving is quite remarkable," one analyst said.
"Shareholders are clearly enjoying the ride but the point we would also make is that it is still a very tough market."

Despite market expectations, Sterling said he did not expect to see any change to the current, low prices in the Channel. He said P&O Stena Line would rely on cost savings and improved service to boost -- or at least maintain -- its market share.

"All our calculations have been on the assumption that there will be no (rate) change," Sterling said. "It would be quite ridiculous for us to work on the basis in our forward plans that there would be any price increases at all."
Sterling said he expected the merger to be signed and sealed with all the necessary approvals before Britain's general election next year and ahead of the peak season next summer.
Market analysts, however, were not convinced about prices.
"I think that post the refinancing of Eurotunnel it's highly unlikely that rates stay down in the bargain basement where they have been this year," Selwyn Jones of Credit Lyonnais Lang said.
"It's been no good for Eurotunnel and no good for P&O/Stena." ($1=.6388 Pound)
